title: How did half the viewers miss a gorilla?
hook: A gorilla walked right through the video. Plenty of people swore it didn’t.
summary: Busy counting passes, about half of viewers missed a gorilla in the video: inattentional blindness (Simons and Chabris, 1999).

cardBlocks.text: In a short video, two teams, one in white shirts and one in black, pass basketballs around. The task is to count only the white team’s passes. Midway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks in, stops in the middle of the scene, thumps its chest and walks off, about nine seconds later.

In Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris’s experiment, published in 1999, about half of the people busy counting passes did not see the gorilla. When they watched again, many accused the researchers of switching the video. The effect is called inattentional blindness: someone focused on one task can fail to notice something unexpected right in front of them.
With attention locked on a task, even a gorilla can go unnoticed: that is inattentional blindness.

deepDiveBlocks.text: We have a strong intuition that anything unexpected and striking in front of us will grab our attention on its own. That is why the result is so startling: people who saw the gorilla can’t believe anyone missed it, and people who missed it can’t believe they did.
When focused on one task, such as talking on a phone while driving, many of us become blind to events around us.
The study was a new version of earlier experiments by the psychologist Ulric Neisser in the 1970s.
